Which NDT Method Should You Learn First?

UT, RT, MT, PT, VT, ET — six letters, six very different starting points. A practical comparison of training hours, industry demand, and learning difficulty to help you pick your first NDT method.

By Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III · August 11, 2026

You Don't Have to Pick All of Them at Once

If you've read our beginner's guide to NDT, you know there isn't one single "NDT machine" — there are several distinct methods, each suited to different defects, materials, and situations. The good news for someone just starting out: you don't certify in all of them at once. Most technicians start with one or two accessible methods and add more as their career develops. The question is which one to start with, and that decision comes down to three practical factors — how much training it takes to get in the door, how much demand exists for it, and how hard it actually is to learn.

Training Hours by Method: The Fastest Entry Points

Under SNT-TC-1A, the classroom-hour requirement to reach Level I varies significantly by method — and this is the most concrete, comparable number available before you commit to any of them. Per the table on our NDT Level 1 training guide:

  • Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT) and Visual Testing (VT) — 8 classroom hours, 130 on-the-job experience hours. The shortest, lowest-equipment-complexity entry points into the field.
  • Magnetic Particle Testing (MT) — 12 classroom hours, 130 on-the-job experience hours. Slightly more involved than PT/VT but still a fast, low-cost entry.
  • Ultrasonic Testing (UT), Radiographic Testing (RT), and Eddy Current Testing (ET) — each 40 classroom hours, 210 on-the-job experience hours. Longer to reach Level I, and more equipment- and physics-intensive to learn.

If your priority is simply getting certified in something as fast as possible — to open the first door into the industry — PT or VT is the objectively fastest path by the numbers.

Which Method Has the Broadest Industry Demand

Training speed isn't the only consideration, though — you also want to know which method gives you the most consistent work once you're certified. Visual Testing is genuinely foundational: it's usually the very first certification a new technician earns, because every other method builds on top of a solid VT foundation, and it's used across every industry that touches NDT at all. But for depth of ongoing demand specifically, Ultrasonic Testing tends to carry the strongest and most consistent pull across industries — it's the workhorse method for wall-thickness and corrosion monitoring in oil & gas and petrochemical work (the largest single employer of NDT technicians), and it shows up heavily in aerospace, power generation, and manufacturing as well. That's why many technicians who start with an accessible method like PT or VT prioritize adding UT next, once they have a foundation certification and some field experience under their belt.

Which Method Is Hardest to Learn First

Difficulty and training hours track each other fairly closely, but not perfectly. Ultrasonic Testing and Radiographic Testing are generally considered the steepest learning curves for a total beginner: UT requires building real intuition for how sound waves behave and reflect inside a material, which takes hands-on repetition to internalize, and RT carries the added layer of radiation safety procedures on top of image interpretation. Eddy Current Testing sits in a similar category — understanding how induced currents respond to material changes isn't intuitive on day one. By contrast, Liquid Penetrant, Visual, and Magnetic Particle testing are more procedural and visually direct: you apply a process and look for a visible indication, which is a more learnable starting point for someone with zero prior technical background. This is exactly why they double as both the fastest and the most beginner-friendly entry point.

A Practical Way to Decide

  • Want the fastest realistic entry into a paying NDT role? Start with PT, VT, or MT — short classroom hours, direct visual interpretation, lower equipment complexity.
  • Already have an employer or industry in mind that runs mostly one method? Match your first certification to what that employer actually needs — a company doing pipeline thickness monitoring wants UT technicians, not PT specialists, regardless of which method is "easier" in the abstract.
  • Optimizing for long-term demand across the widest range of industries? Plan to add Ultrasonic Testing early in your career, even if you start somewhere else first — it's the method with the broadest pull across oil & gas, aerospace, power, and manufacturing.
  • Not sure yet and just want a foundation? Visual Testing is the closest thing NDT has to a universal starting certification, and it's rarely wasted effort since every other method assumes VT-level inspection habits anyway.

Whichever you choose, the entry requirements don't change: no degree, no prior NDT experience, and a passing vision screening, as detailed on our Level I certification guide. Most working technicians end up certified in two to four methods over time — the first one is just the door you walk through, not the ceiling.

Frequently Asked Questions

Q1: What is the easiest NDT method to learn first?

A: Visual Testing (VT) and Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT) are generally the most accessible entry points — shorter classroom hours (8 hours each under SNT-TC-1A) and more direct, visually interpretable results than methods like Ultrasonic or Radiographic Testing.

Q2: Which NDT method should I learn if I want the most job security?

A: Ultrasonic Testing tends to have the broadest and most consistent demand across industries, particularly oil & gas and petrochemical work. It's not the fastest or easiest method to start with, but it's a strong method to prioritize early in your career for that reason.

Q3: Can I learn more than one method at the same time?

A: Most beginners focus on one method first to reach Level I, then add a second once they have some field footing. It's possible to pursue two methods in parallel if your employer supports it, but the on-the-job experience hours for each method still have to be logged separately.

Q4: Does starting with an "easier" method limit my career later?

A: No. Starting with PT, VT, or MT doesn't cap your progression — most working NDT technicians hold certifications in two to four methods, and there's no rule requiring you to start with the hardest one. Many people deliberately start easy to get into paid work faster, then add UT or RT once they have income and experience.
